doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Archival live tapes from clubs and compilations
summary: Dorn describes assembling live tapes of Blakey, Dorham and others, and releasing Joe Williams, Getz and Ray Bryant material. He values the unselfconscious sound.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: The Chinese say, “the long way is the short way.”
But I can just picture you, you must have to sit and do an awful lot of listening, to do reissues.
I learned patience, yeah. Well they’re not — I think what you’re talking about is not necessarily reissues. Reissues to me are when you take an album that was on vinyl and now you put it on CD.
Yeah, that’s not what I mean.

Yeah. No. I got a stash of tapes that no one’s ever heard. I have a way that I do compilations. I have this little area, I started playing it because when I came back after that slump in the early eighties I had to come up with something new. Because the pop records I was making and the jazz records I was making, nobody really wanted. So, this

is too long a story to bore you with but through a friend, Bernie Dreighton, I found some tapes he had made at a small club in Brooklyn in the sixties: Blakey, Kenny Dorham, you know, people like that, guys who’d play these small clubs in Brooklyn to work out material before they recorded for Blue Note or Prestige or stuff like that. So in trying to clear those, I came across other collections. At a certain point we had isolated a quarter of a million hours of privately — in lieu of the word illegally — recorded tapes from concerts, from radio stations, from club owners, from guys that hid microphones in heating ducts, you know. And I started doing this archival work. And I put together lots of stuff, like the stuff I did for you with Joe. ‘Cause you called Nat Hentoff and you said, ‘I got all this Joe Williams stuff,” and Nat said, “Call Joel.” You and I spoke the next thing we know we have “Havin’ a Good Time” with Joe Williams. So it’s like that. So I have all these tapes that I either have stashed or have access to and I thought it was interesting because those live tapes, 99 percent of the time were recorded with the artist not knowing they were being recorded or if they were it was like, “can I record this so I can listen to it at home?” “Yeah, go ahead, kid,” you know that kind of thing. And now you find that that is the least self-conscious recorded music I’ve ever heard because it wasn’t like you’re making a record for Blue Note live, you’ve got two nights — Rudy VanGelder has his eight track out behind the bar. It’s not like that. So it’s as close as I could ever get to what it was really like in those clubs in those times because those jazz clubs were incredible. Those dumps that everybody played and complained about? That’s where the music was magic. That’s where it was created. So all those things you like that we did, the “Left Bank Collection” and the Ray Bryant stuff and the Stan Getz, all that stuff, those tapes are to me the best documentation of what happened in those clubs back then and what those musicians were like on any given night.
I noticed that when I was listening to the Cannonball thing you sent, “Radio Nights.” I’m listening to him and I’ve not heard that kind of playing on even his best records. It was somehow—
It was — all his live records except for two of them were made in the studio with an audience.
Right. They were live studio records.
And you’re right, there was something about it.

There’s a difference. Oh no there’s a real difference. Like if you listen to that Stan Getz record we made, “My Foolish Heart,” you never heard Getz play like that in the studio. That Ray Bryant album we have, the solo piano thing in France, that’s some of the best

solo piano work ever recorded. And I can talk about these records and take myself out of the mix. I had nothing to do with the recording. I put them together, so if I say this is fabulous, it’s fabulous, because the material is fabulous, not because I touched it.
